Russian has no perfect tenses, so an attempt that began earlier and is still going on is simply the present: "мы пытаемся". Everything English packs into "we have been trying" is carried here by the words that follow.
After "пытаться" the verb stays in the infinitive. "Второго дизайнера" is animate, so the accusative copies the genitive: both the ordinal and the noun take those endings.
"С" plus the genitive marks a starting point: "с февраля". The same preposition with the instrumental would mean "together with", so the case is what separates the two meanings.
"Каждый" always takes a singular noun and agrees with it in gender: "каждый кандидат", "каждая встреча".

"Который" is the all-purpose relative pronoun and, unlike English "that", can never be dropped. It agrees in gender and number with the noun it refers to, but takes its case from its own clause — here the nominative, as the subject of "нравился".

"Успевать" means "to manage in time" and has no single-word English equivalent. The imperfective here describes something that happened again and again, which is why "уже" does the work of the English past perfect.
"Эйчары" is a colloquial borrowing for HR staff, and it is plural, so the verb is plural too. "Постоянно" stands before the verb.
The conjunction "что" is compulsory in Russian and always takes a comma before it — unlike English, which drops "that" freely.
"Наверное" is parenthetical and takes commas on both sides: it can be removed without breaking the sentence, which is exactly the test for those commas.
"И всё же" means "still, and yet" as a contrast. It is not the same as "всё ещё", which means "still" in the sense of continuing.
"Подозревать" opens a subordinate clause with "что" and a compulsory comma.

"Процесс у нас" puts the possessor in a "у" phrase instead of using a possessive adjective — a very common Russian turn where English would say "our process". "Слишком" means "too much" as opposed to "очень".
"Быть способным" plus the infinitive is a slightly formal way of saying "can". "Быстрее чем за две недели" uses "за" plus the accusative for the time within which something is done.
"Странно удивляться" is an impersonal construction: there is no subject at all, and the infinitive follows the neuter short form.
In a "когда" clause Russian does use the future when the sense is future, unlike English. "Уходить к другим" means moving to another employer.
The subject in the nominative, with no article: nothing but the context marks it as "the report".
"Должен был быть готов" strings together the modal, the past of "быть" and a short-form adjective. All three agree with the masculine "отчёт".
Days of the week take "в" plus the accusative: "в понедельник", written in lower case.
"Никто не упомянул" needs both negative words: Russian requires the double negation that English forbids.
"Данные" exists only in the plural and takes a plural verb, unlike English "data".
"Браться из" plus the genitive means "to come from". After "трёх" the noun and adjective both go into the genitive plural.
"Их объединение" is a verbal noun where English uses a gerund. Russian builds these freely from verbs, and the object becomes a possessive: "их".
"Занять" is perfective, "to take up time". "Почти всю неделю" is the accusative of duration, with no preposition.
"Половина цифр" puts the counted noun in the genitive. "Всё равно" means "anyway, still", and "не сошлась" agrees with the feminine "половина", not with "цифр".
"В итоге" means "in the end".
"Его" is the accusative of "он", standing for the report, and it comes before the verb here for rhythm — Russian word order is free enough to allow it.
"С примечанием" uses "с" plus the instrumental. "О расхождениях" uses "о" plus the prepositional for the topic.
"К моему удивлению" uses "к" plus the dative and is set off by a comma. It is a fixed phrase.
"Никто не задал" repeats the compulsory double negation. "Задать вопрос" is the fixed collocation; "спросить вопрос" is wrong.
"Ни одного вопроса" is the genitive after a negated verb, and "ни" strengthens the negation. "По ним" uses "по" plus the dative for "about them".
"Никогда не был" again needs both negatives. The past of "быть" is used because Russian only drops the verb in the present tense.
"Особенно" softens the negation. "Хорош" is a short-form adjective, which is what Russian uses in predicates of this kind.
"Быть хорош в чём-то" takes "в" plus the prepositional. "Светская беседа" is the standard rendering of "small talk".
"На конференциях" takes "на", not "в" — the fixed choice for events. The plural with no article means conferences in general.
"Оказываться" means "to end up somewhere". The imperfective describes what regularly happens.
"Где-то" means "somewhere" and softens the statement. "У кофемашины" uses "у" plus the genitive for "right by".
"Кто-нибудь" is the indefinite "someone" for a hypothetical person; "кто-то" would suggest a particular one. "Сам" here means "of their own accord".
"Заводить разговор" is a fixed collocation, literally "to wind up a conversation". "Начинать разговор" is possible but flatter.
"Знакомиться с" takes the instrumental: "с человеком". "По-настоящему" is written with a hyphen and means "genuinely".
"Чаще" is the comparative of "часто", formed with "-е" and a consonant change.
"Просто" means "just, simply" and stands before the verb. "Выпивать" is imperfective, for something that happens repeatedly.
"Много" always takes the genitive: "плохого кофе". Note that "кофе" itself is indeclinable, so only the adjective shows the case.
"Это стратегия" has no verb: the present tense of "быть" is not used.
"С очевидными изъянами" uses "с" plus the instrumental plural. "Изъян" is a bookish word for a flaw.
"Другой у меня нет" uses the genitive with "нет" — the compulsory case in negative existential sentences. The adjective stands alone for "another one", with no noun needed.
"Наша команда" is the subject in the nominative, with the possessive agreeing in the feminine.
"Перейти на" plus the accusative means "to switch to". "Удалёнка" is a colloquial noun for remote work.
"За одну ночь" uses "за" plus the accusative for the time within which something happens. "Почти" softens it.
"Сначала" means "at first" and contrasts with what came later.
"Все" is plural in Russian and takes a plural verb, unlike English "everyone", which is singular.
"Что это временно" has no verb at all: "временно" is a neuter short form used as a predicate. Russian does not shift the tense in reported speech the way English does.
"Спустя" follows the period it refers to: "два года спустя". Before it, "спустя два года", it also works, and both are correct.
"Используется" has "-ся" and forms the passive: the doer is not named. "В основном" means "mostly".
"Для" always takes the genitive: "для встреч", "для печенья". One preposition covers both nouns.
"Сама работа" uses "сам" to emphasise the noun, agreeing with it in gender: "сама" for the feminine "работа".
"Почти не изменилась" places "почти" before the negation. "Измениться" has "-ся" and is intransitive.
"А вот" marks a contrast and introduces something new. "Дорога до офиса" uses "до" plus the genitive.
"Никто" as a negative pronoun, which will require "не" with the verb further on.
"Из моих знакомых" uses "из" plus the genitive to select from a group. "Знакомый" is an adjective used as a noun.
"Не хочет возвращаться" completes the double negation with "никто". After "хотеть" the verb stays in the infinitive, and the imperfective suits a general wish.
"Мой арендодатель" is the subject in the nominative. The word is formal; "хозяин квартиры" is the everyday equivalent.
"Поднять" is perfective. "Аренду" is the accusative of "аренда", which here means the rent rather than the lease.
"На" plus the accusative expresses the size of an increase: "на десять процентов". After "десять" the noun goes into the genitive plural.
"Объяснить" opens a subordinate clause with "что" and a comma. The person told would go into the dative: "объяснил мне".
"Расходы на обслуживание" uses "на" plus the accusative to say what the costs are for. Russian links the two nouns with a preposition where English simply puts them side by side.
"Вырасти" is perfective and intransitive: the costs went up by themselves.
The subject in the nominative, with no article: nothing marks "лифт" as "the lift".
"Не работает с ноября" keeps the present tense: the state still holds, and Russian sees no reason to shift it. English would need a perfect here.
"Что" without a preceding noun refers to the whole previous clause, and the comma before it is compulsory. "Слегка" means "slightly".
"Вежливо" is an adverb and stands before the verb, where English would put it after.
"Входит ли" uses the particle "ли" to build an indirect yes-or-no question. It comes second in the clause, right after the word being questioned.
"Его починка" is a verbal noun with a possessive, where English uses a gerund with an object: "fixing it". This noun is the subject of "входит".
"Сказать" is perfective and opens a clause with "что". The person told goes into the dative.
"Посмотрит" is a perfective future, so no auxiliary is needed. Here the verb is used figuratively, "will look into it".
"А" contrasts with what came before and is not the same as "и". Russian uses guillemets for quotation, and the comma goes outside them.
"Записаться" has "-ся": you sign yourself up. It is perfective, describing one completed act.
"На марафон" uses "на" plus the accusative, the preposition Russian uses for events you sign up for.
"В порыве энтузиазма" uses "в" plus the prepositional for the state one is in. "Энтузиазма" is the genitive after "порыве".
"Тренировки" is plural here, where English "training" is uncountable and singular. The verb must therefore be plural too.
"Идти" is used figuratively for how something is going, exactly as English "go" is.
"Лучше" is the irregular comparative of "хорошо". After "чем" comes a full clause with its own subject and verb, and the comma before "чем" is compulsory.
The subject in the nominative: "проблема" needs no article and no verb after it.
"Проблема в том, что" is a fixed frame: "в том" is the prepositional, and the comma before "что" cannot be dropped. "Говорить о" takes the prepositional: "о беге".
"Постоянно" at the end of the clause carries more weight than it would in the middle.
The nominative plural as the subject. Russian often drops the possessive where English needs one: "друзья" alone reads as "my friends".
After "начать" the verb stays in the infinitive, and the imperfective "менять" describes a repeated action. "Менять тему" is the fixed collocation.
"Ещё до того, как" is a three-part conjunction, and the comma inside it is compulsory. The perfective future "открою" describes the moment the action would begin.
"Видимо" is parenthetical and means "apparently". It is usually set off by a comma.
"Есть предел тому" uses the dative "тому" because "предел" governs it. Russian needs this pointing word before the clause that follows.
"Сколько" opens an indirect question. "Способен" is a short-form adjective followed by an infinitive, and "про" is the colloquial equivalent of "о".
"Новую систему" is the accusative object standing first — Russian word order is free, and putting the object first here highlights it.
A subjectless plural verb where English uses the passive: "внедрили" means "they introduced it", with no "they" named.
"Без" always takes the genitive: "без предупреждения".
"Нам сказали" is another subjectless plural. The person told goes into the dative, "нам".
"Сэкономит" is a perfective future. Russian keeps the future here, where English shifts to "would" by the sequence of tenses.
"Каждому" is the dative, because "сэкономить" takes the person in that case. "Около часа" uses the genitive after "около".
"Пока что" means "so far". Russian has no perfect tense to pair with it.
"Породить" is perfective and slightly bookish, "to give rise to". "В основном" means "mostly".
"Новые виды совещаний" puts the counted noun in the genitive plural after "виды".
"Справедливости ради" is a fixed phrase with the genitive and a postposed "ради". It is set off by a comma.
The subject in the nominative. Note the lower-case letter: "интерфейс" starts a new clause after a comma, not a new sentence.
"Стать" plus a comparative means "to become better". "Действительно" means "genuinely" and stands before the comparative.
"Оправдывает ли" uses the particle "ли" for a yes-or-no question, and here the whole question is the subject of what follows.
"Полгода" is written as one word and takes the genitive after it: "миграции".
There is no verb: "вопрос отдельный" is a nominal predicate, and the dash before it stands in for the missing "is".
"Мой сосед" is the subject in the nominative.
Three verbs in a row: a perfective past, then two infinitives. "Играть на трубе" uses "на" plus the prepositional for instruments.
"В пятьдесят два" uses "в" plus the accusative for age. English uses "at" here, and the preposition simply differs.
"Первый месяц" is the accusative of duration, with no preposition.
"Честно говоря" is a fixed parenthetical phrase built on a verbal adverb, and it takes commas on both sides.
"Тяжеловато" is a diminutive adverb: the suffix softens the judgement to "a bit hard". This is an impersonal construction with an infinitive and no subject.
"Почти" means "very nearly". "Сделать замечание" is the fixed collocation for saying something critical.
"А потом" marks the turn in the story. "Вспомнить" is perfective and opens a clause.
"Как ужасно пою" places the adverb before the verb. "Сам" adds "myself" and agrees with the implied subject.
"С лета" uses "с" plus the genitive for a starting point, as in the first phrase. The season needs no article or adjective.
"Вырасти" is used figuratively for improvement, exactly as it is for growth. "Невероятно" follows the verb.
"Почему-то" means "for some reason" and is written with a hyphen. "Гордиться" always takes the instrumental: "им".
"Теперь" opens the contrast with the past.
"По воскресеньям" uses "по" plus the dative plural for a regular day. This is the standard way Russian says "on Sundays".
"Казаться" takes the instrumental for what something seems to be: "странной", agreeing with the feminine "тишина".
"Обычно" stands between the subject and the negation. Russian places the negative particle immediately before the verb it negates.
"Доверять" always takes the dative: "советам". "Про" is the colloquial equivalent of "о" and takes the accusative.
"Потому что" is a two-part conjunction, and the comma may go before either half depending on emphasis. "Сами себе" is the reflexive pronoun in the dative, required by "противоречить".
"Одна книга" here means "one book" in contrast with the next, not simply "a book".
"Велит" is a bookish verb meaning "orders, tells to". After it comes an infinitive, and the imperfective "начинать" fits a general instruction.
"С самой трудной задачи" uses "с" plus the genitive for a starting point. "Самый" builds the superlative and agrees with the noun.
An adjective used as a noun, "the next one". Russian needs no equivalent of English "one".
"Настаивать" opens a clause with "что" and a compulsory comma.
"Надо разогнаться" is impersonal: no subject, and the infinitive follows. "Разогнаться" is used figuratively for building up momentum.
"То, что" is a two-part frame, and the comma inside it is compulsory. "Сработало" is perfective, and "у меня" says for whom.
"Гораздо" intensifies a comparative. "Скучнее" is formed with "-ее" from "скучный".
"Меньше вкладок" takes the genitive after the quantity word. "Пораньше" is a softened comparative: the prefix "по-" makes it "a bit earlier".
"Никто" as the negative pronoun, which will pull "не" to the verb.
"Стать" plus an imperfective infinitive means "to be going to", and the negation makes it "nobody will". The double negation with "никто" is compulsory.
"Книгу об этом" is the accusative object plus "о" with the prepositional. Before a vowel the preposition becomes "об".
"Предупреждать" is imperfective: the warnings were repeated. "Нас" is the accusative — this verb takes the person directly.
"Про этот дедлайн" uses the colloquial "про" plus the accusative. "Дедлайн" is a recent borrowing and declines like any masculine noun.
"Неделями" is the instrumental plural used for a long stretch of repeated time. It is a compact construction English has to unpack into "for weeks".
"Кивали" is imperfective past: the nodding happened again and again.
"На каждой встрече" uses "на" plus the prepositional, and "каждый" agrees with the feminine noun.
"Не меняли ничего" needs both negative words, as always in Russian.
"Когда" opens a subordinate clause of time, with a compulsory comma before it.
"Сдвинуть вперёд" about a date means to bring it earlier. The direction is not obvious from the words and simply has to be learned.
"Выйти" plus the instrumental means "to turn out to be": "вышла впечатляющей". The instrumental is what makes this construction work.
"Каким-то образом" is a fixed instrumental phrase meaning "somehow".
"Всё сдали" uses "всё" as the object. "Сдать" is perfective, "to hand in and have it accepted".
"В ту самую пятницу" uses "в" plus the accusative, and "тот самый" means "that very one". All three words agree in the feminine accusative.
"Ни разу" needs "не" with the verb further on. "Ни" strengthens the negation and cannot stand alone.
The double negation begun by "ни разу" is completed here by "не сказала". Russian uses guillemets for direct speech inside a sentence, and no inversion of any kind takes place.
"Именно поэтому" means "that is exactly why". "Её слушают все" puts the object first — free word order lets Russian foreground what matters, without changing the case endings.
